kinetic-control-s1.title: Three reactions at 298 K
kinetic-control-s1.text: A student compares three reactions at 298 K. Each is mixed under standard conditions and watched for one hour.

table.caption: Free energy change, activation energy and what is observed

kinetic-control-s2.title: Two pathways from one starting material
kinetic-control-s2.text: Compound A can turn into either of two products. The energy profile below compares the two pathways at 25 °C.
kinetic-control-s2.html: Key: solid line, pathway to B (barrier 40 kJ/mol, ΔG° = −20 kJ/mol); dashed line, pathway to C (barrier 110 kJ/mol, ΔG° = −60 kJ/mol). Barriers are measured from A.

items.q: Which reactions in the table are thermodynamically favored at 298 K?
options: Reaction 2 alone, because it is the one that is observed
All three
Reactions 2 and 3, because their ΔG° values are large
No reaction in the table, because two show no change

why.correct: Favorability depends on the sign of ΔG° alone. All three have ΔG° < 0.
options: Being observed is about rate. Favorability is decided by the sign of ΔG°, which is negative for all three.
Right: every ΔG° is negative, so every reaction is favored, whether or not it is fast.
Any negative ΔG° means favored; −2.9 kJ/mol counts too.
A reaction can be favored and still too slow to see.

items.q: Which statement best explains why Reaction 3 shows no change in an hour?
options: Its ΔG° is positive at 298 K, so the mixture has to be heated before water can form.
The mixture is already at equilibrium, so no further change can occur.
The reaction absorbs too much heat from the surroundings to proceed.
Its activation energy is large, so few H₂–O₂ collisions have enough energy to react.

why.correct: A favored reaction with a large activation energy is too slow to observe: it is under kinetic control.
options: ΔG° is −474.2 kJ/mol, strongly negative. The problem is the rate, not favorability.
With ΔG° this negative, equilibrium lies almost entirely on the product side; the mixture is far from it.
Forming water from H₂ and O₂ releases a large amount of heat.
Right: the reaction is under kinetic control. It is favored, but the rate is negligible.

items.q: A spark is passed through the mixture in Reaction 3 and it reacts explosively. What does the spark do?
options: It gets some molecules over the barrier; the heat they release lets others react.
It changes ΔG° from positive to negative, which makes the reaction favored.
It lowers the activation energy permanently, the way a catalyst does.
It shifts the equilibrium constant to favor products for as long as the spark lasts.

why.correct: The barrier, not ΔG°, kept the mixture unreacted. A spark supplies enough energy to start the reaction, and the energy it releases keeps it going.
options: Right: the spark supplies the activation energy to start; the exothermic reaction then supplies its own.
ΔG° was already negative; the spark changes the rate, not the thermodynamics.
A spark adds energy; it does not provide a new pathway, so Ea is unchanged.
K depends on temperature, not on a spark, and was already very large.

items.q: Diamonds kept for centuries do not turn into graphite. Which statement is correct?
options: Diamond is thermodynamically more stable than graphite at 298 K.
The conversion is not favored, because its ΔG° is small.
Diamond is kinetically stable: the change is favored but has a huge Ea.
The conversion is at equilibrium, so equal amounts of diamond and graphite are present.

why.correct: Kinetic stability (a slow rate) and thermodynamic stability (the sign of ΔG°) are different. Diamond is the first, not the second.
options: ΔG° for diamond → graphite is negative, so graphite is the more stable form.
A small negative ΔG° is still negative: the conversion is favored, just slowly.
Right: ΔG° < 0, yet breaking and rearranging the strong covalent network is extremely slow.
There is no graphite forming at a measurable rate, so this is not an equilibrium mixture.

items.q: Which product is thermodynamically favored more strongly?
options: B, because its barrier is lower
B, because it is the product that forms first
C, because its ΔG° is more negative
Neither, because both reactions are endothermic

why.correct: The product with the more negative ΔG° is thermodynamically favored. That is C.
options: A lower barrier means a faster reaction, not a more favored product.
Which product forms first is a question of rate, not of thermodynamics.
Right: −60 kJ/mol is more negative than −20 kJ/mol, so C is the more stable product.
Both pathways go downhill in free energy; both products are favored.

items.q: At 25 °C, A is mostly converted to B within minutes, and almost no C forms in that time. Which explanation is best?
options: The barrier to B is much lower, so many more collisions reach B: kinetic control.
B is thermodynamically more stable than C, so the reaction stops at B.
C does not form, because a barrier of 110 kJ/mol is impossible to cross at 25 °C.
B forms because its ΔG° is closer to zero, so less energy has to be released.

why.correct: Rate depends on activation energy. B has the lower barrier, so it forms faster: the result is controlled by kinetics, not by which product is more stable.
options: Right: the faster product forms first, even though C is more stable.
C has the more negative ΔG°, so C is the more stable product.
High barriers can be crossed; they are crossed slowly. Given time or heat, C can form.
How much energy is released does not decide which product forms faster; the barrier height does.

items.q: A chemist wants mostly C. Which change is most likely to help, and why?
options: Cool the mixture, because a lower temperature favors the product with the larger barrier.
Stop the reaction after a few minutes, before C has had a chance to break down.
Add more A, because a higher concentration lowers the activation energy for C.
Heat it for a long time, so collisions can cross the larger barrier to C.

why.correct: To get the thermodynamic product, give the system enough energy and time to cross the larger barrier.
options: Cooling slows every pathway, the high-barrier one most of all.
After a few minutes the mixture is mostly B, not C.
Concentration changes the rate through collision frequency, not the barrier height.
Right: higher T and more time let the slow pathway to the more stable C catch up.

items.q: Which statement compares the two pathways correctly?
options: Formation of B is faster and more favored.
Formation of B is faster; formation of C is more favored.
Formation of C is faster and more favored.
The two pathways have the same rate, because they start from the same compound.

why.correct: Rate follows the barrier (Ea); favorability follows ΔG°. Here they point to different products.
options: B is faster, but C has the more negative ΔG°.
Right: the lower barrier makes B faster; the more negative ΔG° makes C more favored.
C has the higher barrier, so its formation is slower.
Rates depend on the barriers, which differ: 40 vs 110 kJ/mol.

items.q: What does a negative ΔG° tell you about a reaction?
options: It is favored, but it may be fast or very slow.
It will happen quickly once the reactants are mixed.
It has a small activation energy barrier.
It needs a continuous input of energy to keep going.

why.correct: Thermodynamics (ΔG°) answers "can it go?"; kinetics (Ea) answers "how fast?".
options: Right: ΔG° says whether a reaction can go on its own, not how fast.
ΔG° says nothing about rate; rate depends on the activation energy.
ΔG° and Ea are independent; a very favored reaction can have a huge barrier.
That describes a process with ΔG° > 0.

items.q: Paper burns in air with ΔG° far below zero, yet a book can sit on a shelf for a hundred years. Which explanation is best?
options: ΔG° for burning paper becomes positive at room temperature.
Paper is at equilibrium with the oxygen in the air.
Burning paper has a large Ea, so at 25 °C its rate is negligible.
There is not enough oxygen in the air for the reaction to be favored.

why.correct: Favored processes can be kinetically stable when the activation energy is large.
options: Combustion has ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° > 0, so ΔG° is negative at every temperature.
Equilibrium would lie almost entirely on the side of CO₂ and H₂O; the book is far from it.
Right: it is favored, but under kinetic control at 298 K.
Air holds plenty of oxygen; the reaction is favored but slow.

items.q: Adding a catalyst to a reaction that is under kinetic control has which effect?
options: It makes ΔG° more negative, so the reaction becomes more favored.
It lowers Ea so the reaction can run at a measurable rate; ΔG° stays the same.
It makes a reaction with ΔG° > 0 favored.
It raises the activation energy of the reverse reaction alone, so products build up.

why.correct: A catalyst changes the pathway and Ea, so it changes the rate. It cannot change ΔG°, ΔH° or K.
options: ΔG° depends on the reactants and products, which a catalyst does not change.
Right: a catalyst provides a lower-barrier pathway but does not change the starting or ending free energies.
A catalyst cannot make an unfavored reaction favored; it speeds both directions equally.
A catalyst lowers the barrier in both directions.

items.q: A student mixes two solutions, sees no reaction after an hour, and concludes "ΔG° for this reaction must be positive." Which reply is best?
options: That is correct, because any reaction with ΔG° < 0 happens within minutes.
That is correct, because a reaction that does not happen has ΔG° = 0.
That does not follow, because ΔG° is negative for any reaction that releases heat.
It does not follow: a favored reaction can be too slow to see; ΔG° comes from data.

why.correct: An observation of no change cannot separate "not favored" from "favored but slow". You need ΔG° data to decide.
options: Many favored reactions are extremely slow (diamond to graphite, paper burning at room temperature).
ΔG° = 0 means neither direction is favored under standard conditions; it is not what "no visible change" shows.
Not so: an exothermic reaction with ΔS° < 0 can have ΔG° > 0 at high temperature.
Right: no visible change could mean ΔG° > 0 or could mean a large Ea.

items.q: Which are examples of a thermodynamically favored process that is under kinetic control at room temperature? Select ALL that apply.
options: Methane and oxygen in a gas stove before it is lit
An iron nail that rusts only over months
Ice melting on a kitchen counter at 25 °C
Water decomposing into hydrogen and oxygen in a closed bottle

why.correct: Kinetic control means ΔG° < 0 but a rate too slow to see. The gas stove and the nail fit; ice melts readily, and water decomposition is not favored at all.
options: Favored (combustion) but slow until a flame supplies the activation energy.
Favored, but the rate is slow at room temperature.
Favored and happens at a visible rate, so it is not under kinetic control.
Not favored at 25 °C: ΔG° is positive, so it does not happen at any rate.

items.q: Glucose and oxygen react with ΔG° = −2870 kJ/mol, yet sugar in a bowl does not burn. In your cells, enzymes let the same overall reaction run at body temperature. What do the enzymes change?
options: The sign of ΔG°, so the reaction becomes favored in the body
The products of the reaction, so less energy is released
The temperature of the cell, so it reaches the burning point of sugar
The activation energy of each step, so it runs at a useful rate

why.correct: Sugar in a bowl is under kinetic control. Enzymes lower the activation energy, so the favored reaction runs fast enough at body temperature.
options: ΔG° was already very negative; enzymes do not change it.
The overall reaction and its ΔG° are the same in the bowl and in the cell.
Your body stays near 37 °C; enzymes work by lowering barriers, not by heating.
Right: enzymes are catalysts; they lower the barrier without changing ΔG°.

items.q: Which pair of data would show that a reaction at 298 K is under kinetic control?
options: ΔG° = +40 kJ/mol and no measurable product after a week
ΔG° = −150 kJ/mol and no measurable product after a week
ΔG° = −150 kJ/mol and a complete reaction within one second
ΔG° = +40 kJ/mol and complete reaction in one second

why.correct: Kinetic control means ΔG° < 0 (favored) with a rate too small to observe.
options: With ΔG° > 0 the reaction is not favored, so there is no product at any rate.
Right: strongly favored, yet no measurable rate. That combination is the definition.
Favored and fast: this reaction is not held back by kinetics.
A reaction with ΔG° > 0 under standard conditions does not go to completion on its own.
